and NOT `note`, because SwimTeach in src/app/swim/page.tsx renders st.n, st.name, st.who and
st.cues and nothing else. They were written as `note` on 2026-09-02, shipped nowhere, and were
caught by screenshotting the tab at 390px rather than by any gate: a field that reads like
content and reaches no screen is worse than no field, because the next agent believes the stage
explains itself on the page. They are provenance now and are named as such. If a stage rationale
should be VISIBLE to him, that is a page change and a judgement about how much text the tab
carries, which note #12 in AGENTS.md says is his: "Walls of text again why do I need all this".
COACH THEM. Re-sourced 2026-09-02 from Swim England learn-to-swim material, on his ruling, and
the ruling was about SOURCES rather than about sentences:
"I don't know if these two things come from the same source. I think they should be from
different sources."
He had opened both coaching tabs and found them saying the same things. They were: eight of the
nine cues on this tab quoted the same four US Masters Swimming freestyle guides that Coach me
quotes, and validate.mjs counted SIX sentences cited on both tabs. Editing the six sentences to
differ would have left one source feeding two tabs and the overlap would have grown back, so the
fix is at the source: this tab now quotes learn-to-swim pages only, and Coach me keeps USMS.
WHAT THAT COST, said plainly because it is not free. Learn-to-swim material does not teach the
model USMS teaches. There is no seesaw, no "press the chest down and the hips come up", no
early-elbow catch and no kick-starts-at-the-hip. Swim England teaches beginners to stretch long,
keep the legs long with loose ankles and kick continuously, pull each arm through to the thigh in
one continuous cycle, and turn the head inside the bow wave. So the CUES CHANGED, not just their
citations. Keeping the old cues and swapping in quotes that do not support them is the exact
failure content/swim/capture-source.mjs names in its own header: a sentence above a quote that
the quote does not carry. A quote is evidence for the sentence it is under or it is decoration.
NOTHING WAS LOST, IT MOVED TO THE RIGHT TAB. The two observations dropped from whatToLookFor,
the splashing kick and the straight-arm pull, are the USMS model and they are still on Coach me,
which is where a competitive guide belongs. This tab is for the person being taught.
WHO IT IS FOR, his words: "really beginners that have never actually swum to friends that swim
kind of weakly, on and off, and they want to focus more on form and understanding the concept."
Swim England publishes a framework for exactly that population and this tab is now built on it.
THE DISCLAIMER IS GONE, per his ruling: "We don't need the disclaimer, whatever, like that thing
that I'm not coaching. We know that already." The credentials half of beforeYouStart is out. The
WATER-SAFETY half is still there and was NOT treated as covered by that ruling, because it is a

STAGE IDS: one changed. "catch" became "arms", because no cue in it mentions a catch any more and

--- the record before 2026-09-02 ---
THE TEACHING HANDBOOK. Built 2026-08-22 from his own problem, in his words:
'Sometimes people approach me when I'm swimming or just outside the pool, or just friends,
and ask me if I can teach them how to swim, which I can't... I have no idea how to explain
principles that I'm already familiar with but not sure how to explain.'
'There are a lot of people that I've met at the pool that I go to that ask me some stuff. I'm
not really sure how to tell them what to work on or what to improve.'
AGENTS DO NOT WRITE SWIM INSTRUCTION FROM MEMORY. The same rule the kitchen learned the hard
way on 2026-08-09: every failure there came from a sentence an agent wrote, and not one came
from a figure a source gave. Somebody could get hurt taking bad water advice, so every stage
and every fix below traces to a named source, and the two that do not say so on the page.
THE BACKBONE is Swim England's Learn to Swim framework, which teaches nine core aquatic skills
rather than strokes: entry, exit, floatation, rotation, streamlining, breathing, travel and
coordination, water safety, and fitness. That ordering is why the first two stages here contain
no swimming at all. Someone who cannot float and cannot breathe out underwater does not have a
stroke problem.
THAT COUNT OF NINE IS CORRECT AND WAS OVERWRITTEN ONCE. On 2026-08-22 the sources note below
was changed to say FOUR, with the quote truncated after the fourth bullet, and this paragraph
was left alone. Re-read over CDP on 2026-09-02: the page lists nine. The file disagreed with
itself for eleven days and the half that rendered on his phone was the wrong half.
THE FREESTYLE HALF is US Masters Swimming's own coaching guides: body position, breathing, pull
and kick. A governing body's coaching resource, not a blog, and the phrasing that is quoted is
quoted rather than paraphrased.
EVERY FIX IS A TEST HE CAN WATCH, not a feeling the other person has to have. Same house rule
the kitchen runs on: 'wait until it sizzles rather than hisses' failed, and 'tilt the pan, if
liquid runs it is not ready' replaced it. He is standing on a pool deck looking at somebody. He
needs something he can SEE.
AND THE FIRST PAGE IS A REFUSAL. The most useful thing he can tell a nervous non-swimmer is
that he is not a teacher and deep water is where people drown. That is not modesty, it is the
single highest-stakes sentence in this file.

meta.who: Beginners who have never really swum, through to people who swim weakly and on and off and want the form and the idea behind it.
meta.sourceFamily: Swim England learn-to-swim and Just Swim pages only. US Masters Swimming is Coach me and does not appear here.

beforeYouStart.title: Before you take anyone in the water
body: If they cannot float, cannot put their face in, or are frightened, send them to a class. Do it
in shallow water, do not take a nervous person into deep water to demonstrate anything, and do
not hold anyone up. Drowning is quiet and it is fast.

stages.name: Comfortable, before anything else
stages.who: They can stand in the pool but will not put their face in, or they hold their breath and rush.

cues.name: Breathe OUT under the water
cues.cue: Face in, and let the air out the whole time the face is down. It can trickle out gently or go all at once, through the mouth or the nose or both, whichever they find easier. Come up only to breathe in.
cues.test: Stand next to them and watch for bubbles. Continuous bubbles means they are breathing out. No bubbles means they are holding their breath, which is the thing to fix before anything else.
cues.why: Holding the breath is what makes people panic and rush. The guide says not to hold it, and it deliberately offers two ways of letting it out rather than one, which matters for a beginner who will find one of them impossible.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Just Swim: Improve your breathing in front crawl. The source gives the choice of trickle or explosive and of mouth, nose or both, so the cue gives it too rather than picking one for them.
cues.quote: Make sure you exhale under the water and try not to hold your breath. It may be a trickle (gentle and continuous) or explosive (all in one go). It can be through your mouth, nose or a combination of the two.

cues.name: Float on the front, stretched as long as you can
cues.cue: Face in the water, and stretch out until they are as long as they can make themselves, head to toes. Then do nothing and let the water hold them up.
cues.test: Do they stay up without moving? If the legs sink the moment they stop kicking, they are not floating yet and there is no point talking about a stroke.
cues.why: Floatation and Balance is one of the nine core aquatic skills the Swim England framework names, and it sits ahead of Travel and Coordination in that list. Stretching long is how the learn-to-swim material opens every front-facing stroke, so it is the first thing to build and not a refinement.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Tips for learning the four swimming strokes, front crawl. NOTE ON THIS QUOTE: the same sentence opens the front crawl, breaststroke and butterfly sections of that page, so it is the framework's common starting position for any stroke swum on the front, not a front-crawl detail. Quoted as the general instruction it is.
cues.quote: Float on your front with your face in the water, stretching your body as long as possible.

stages.$note: There is no stroke in this stage on purpose. The Swim England framework teaches the core aquatic skills first and every stroke comes after them.

stages.name: Long, flat, and the legs never stop
stages.who: They can get down a length but it looks like hard work, and the legs drag behind them.

cues.name: Legs long, ankles floppy, kick that never stops
cues.cue: Legs long behind them with the toes pointed away, ankles loose enough to flop, kicking up and down one after the other. Small and fast and continuous, not in bursts. The guide's own image is that the feet are flippers.
cues.test: Watch from the side for one length. Does the kick stop and start, or does it run the whole way? A kick that stops whenever the arms are working is the common version of this and it is what drops the legs.
cues.why: A beginner whose legs sink usually has stiff ankles and a kick that pauses, not a body-position problem. This is where the learn-to-swim material and a competitive guide part company, and this tab follows the learn-to-swim one.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Tips for learning the four swimming strokes, front crawl. "Floppy" and "feet like flippers" are the source's words, kept because they are the kind of instruction a beginner can act on immediately.
cues.quote: Keep your legs long with toes pointed. Kick your legs up and down (alternating) making your ankles as floppy as possible, using your feet like flippers. Kick your legs fast and continuously.

cues.name: The head turns inside the wave, it does not lift forward
cues.cue: The head stays where the water piles up in front of it and turns to the side as the body rolls. It does not come up and forward. There is a pocket of air in that dip and that is what they are breathing from.
cues.test: Watch the head from the side. If it comes UP and forward to breathe, the hips drop on every single breath. If it turns and stays low, they have found the pocket.
cues.why: Telling someone not to lift the head explains nothing about where the air is instead. The source says there is a trough of air in front of the head, which turns a prohibition into somewhere to aim.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Just Swim: Improve your breathing in front crawl. The same page explains the mechanism in the next sentence: "The bow wave will create a trough or pocket of air for you to breathe into, protecting your mouth and nose from the water." Quoted here as the reason rather than as a second cue.
cues.quote: The head stays in the bow wave, and smoothly turns to one side, not lifting forwards, to inhale as the body rotates.

stages.$note: The learn-to-swim answer to dragging legs is not a trick with the chest. It is longer legs, looser ankles, and a kick that does not stop.

stages.name: One continuous arm movement
stages.who: They are flat and relaxed, and the arms stop and start: there is a moment with both hands out in front and nothing happening.

cues.name: As one hand goes in, the other is leaving at the thigh
cues.cue: Each arm pulls all the way under the body to the thigh, comes out, sweeps forward over the water and reaches in again in front of the head. It runs continuously, so at the moment one hand enters, the other should be arriving at the thigh.
cues.test: Watch from the end of the lane. Is there ever a moment with both hands in front of the head? That gap is the thing to remove, and it is easier to see than anything about the shape of the pull.
cues.why: A beginner who pauses with both arms in front stops and restarts the whole body every stroke. Naming where the other hand should be at the moment of entry gives them one checkable instant instead of a description of a whole arm path.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Tips for learning the four swimming strokes, front crawl. The pull goes "all the way to the thigh" in the source, which is the half beginners cut short.
cues.quote: Start with your arms stretched out long in front of your head. Pull one arm under your body all the way to the thigh. Bring your arm out of the water and sweep it over the water stretching it ready to enter the water in front of your head. Keep pulling your arms in a continuous movement so that as one arm enters, the other is ready to exit at the thigh.

cues.name: The front arm waits, extended, while they breathe
cues.cue: When the head turns to breathe, the other arm stays stretched out in front, in line with its own shoulder and a little under the surface, about the length of a forearm down. It waits there until the head is back.
cues.test: From the side, watch the front hand at the moment they breathe. Does it stay out in front, or does it drop and start pulling early to help the head round? The early pull is the common fault and it is what makes a breath cost them a stroke.
cues.why: The breath is where most weak swimmers lose the stroke, and the reason is usually the arm they are not thinking about. The source gives a depth, 20 to 30 cm, which is close enough to a forearm to be usable poolside.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Just Swim: Improve your breathing in front crawl. The 20 to 30 cm and the elbow-above-wrist-above-fingertips ordering are the source's. "About the length of a forearm" is a restatement of the source's figure in something visible without a ruler, and it is flagged here as a restatement rather than a quote.
cues.quote: As you turn your head, keep your opposite arm extended in front of you and in line with your shoulder. It will be about 20-30 cm under the water with your elbow higher than your wrist. Your wrist higher than your finger tips.

stages.$note: This stage was called Holding the water and taught the catch. Learn-to-swim material does not teach a catch, it teaches a cycle that never has a gap in it, so that is what this stage teaches now.

stages.name: Keeping it going
stages.who: The stroke is fine for a length and falls apart over four.

cues.name: Pick the breath cycle before pushing off
cues.cue: Decide before they start: a breath every three arm strokes, or every five. Then hold whichever one they chose for the whole length, instead of breathing when it starts to feel bad.
cues.test: Count their breaths over one length, twice. If the number is different each time, they are breathing on feel and not on a cycle, which is what makes the fourth length fall apart.
cues.why: Breathing on discomfort means the breath arrives later and later as they tire, and the stroke degrades with it. A number chosen in advance is something they can hold to and something a watcher can count.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Just Swim: Improve your breathing in front crawl. NOTE THE NUMBERS: this source says every three or five strokes. It does NOT offer every two, which the Coach me tab discusses at length from a different source and a different population. This tab does not import that argument.
cues.quote: The breath cycle is commonly every three or five arm strokes

cues.name: Breathe on the timing, and keep one ear in the water
cues.cue: The head turns when one arm is stretched out in front and the other is back at the thigh. One ear stays in the water the whole time it turns. As the back arm sweeps over, the face goes back in and the air starts coming out again.
cues.test: Watch from the side: does an ear stay in the water through the breath, or does the whole head clear the surface? The ear is the easiest thing to see from the deck and it is a yes or no.
cues.why: This is the same instruction as the stage-2 head cue, aimed at a different problem: not whether they lift the head but WHEN in the arm cycle they turn it. A breath taken at the wrong moment in the cycle costs the stroke even when the head stays low.
cues.grounding: Swim England, Tips for learning the four swimming strokes, front crawl. "Keep one ear in the water" is the source's own test and it is the reason this quote was chosen over the several other breathing sentences available.
cues.quote: Turn your head to the side to breathe in. Turn as one arm is stretched in front and one at the thigh. Try to keep one ear in the water as you turn your head. As the arm sweeps over the water return your face back into the water and breathe out.

stages.$note: Everything in this stage is about the breath, because that is what decides whether a stroke survives four lengths.

whatToLookFor.title: If they just ask what to work on
whatToLookFor.intro: Watch one length from the side and one from the end. Almost every adult freestyle problem is one of these five, and they are in the order worth fixing.

items.see: Holding their breath, coming up gasping
items.say: Let the air out the whole time your face is down

items.see: Legs low and dragging, lots of effort
items.say: Stretch longer, loosen the ankles, and do not let the kick stop

items.see: Head lifts up and forward to breathe
items.say: Turn it in the dip in front of your head instead of lifting it

items.see: A pause with both hands out in front
items.say: As one hand goes in, the other should be leaving at your thigh

items.see: Fine for one length, wrecked by four
items.say: Choose every three or every five before you push off, and hold it

whatToLookFor.$whatChanged: REBUILT 2026-09-02 with the stages. Two items were the USMS model and went with it: "Big splashing kick, feet out of the water" answered by "Smaller and faster, from the hip, feet just under the surface", and "Straight arm pulling, hand slipping through" answered by "Bend the elbow early and face the palm backwards". Both are still on Coach me, which keeps USMS. They were not deleted for being wrong; they were moved off a tab that no longer cites the guide they came from. sources.label: Swim England Adult Swimming Framework
sources.note: Swim England's framework for adults, four stages, complete beginner through to weak swimmer wanting technique. Cited for who this tab is for.
sources.$note: THE AUDIENCE MATCH IS WHY THIS SOURCE IS HERE. The page describes the framework as "suitable for everyone, from complete beginners to experienced swimmers who would just like some additional coaching to improve their technique", which is close to word for word what he described: "really beginners that have never actually swum to friends that swim kind of weakly, on and off, and they want to focus more on form and understanding the concept." It also states that adults learn differently from children and are taught to different goals, which is the reason a child's learn-to-swim stage list is not the structure used here. NO CUE QUOTES THIS PAGE, because there is no technique on it: it is a programme description. Captured over CDP 2026-09-02.

sources.label: Swim England Learn to Swim, Tips for learning the four swimming strokes
sources.note: Swim England's learn-to-swim stroke instructions, four bullets per stroke in beginner language.
sources.$note: Its opening line places it after the basics rather than at them: "Learning the four swimming strokes comes after you have mastered the basic skills of swimming." Four of the eight cues on this tab quote it. Captured over CDP 2026-09-02. ONE THING TO KNOW BEFORE QUOTING IT AGAIN: the sentence "Float on your front with your face in the water, stretching your body as long as possible." opens the front crawl, breaststroke AND butterfly sections, so it is the framework's common starting position for any stroke swum on the front rather than a front-crawl detail. It is quoted here as the general instruction it is.

sources.label: Swim England Just Swim, Improve your breathing in front crawl
sources.note: Swim England's nine breathing tips for front crawl, and the only source here that gives numbers you can check from the deck.
sources.$note: The checkable numbers are a breath cycle of every three or five strokes and a front arm 20 to 30 cm under the surface. Four of the eight cues on this tab quote it. NOTE THE FREQUENCY: this page offers every three or five and does NOT offer every two, which the Coach me tab argues about at length from a different source and a different population. That argument is deliberately not imported here. Captured over CDP 2026-09-02.

sources.label: Swim England Just Swim, Tips for getting front crawl right
sources.note: Swim England's front crawl tips. Cited only for where front crawl sits in the pathway: stage 3, after the basic skills.
sources.$note:
NO CUE QUOTES THIS PAGE, DELIBERATELY. Its four front-crawl bullets are the same four sentences as se-strokes, so quoting it would put one sentence under two source ids and make one page look like corroboration of the other. It is captured and listed because the pathway sentence is its own: "Learning all the main swimming strokes comes after you have mastered the basic skills of swimming. This is during Stage 3 of the Learn to Swim Pathway for adults learning to swim."

FLAGGED FOR WHOEVER READS IT NEXT: the page carries a copy-paste error of its own, an intro paragraph about being "ready to develop" breaststroke on a front crawl page. Nothing here rests on that sentence. It is recorded because a source with a visible error deserves a note beside it rather than silent trust, and because the next agent to open it should not spend a message wondering whether the capture is of the wrong page. Captured over CDP 2026-09-02.

sources.label: Swim England Learn to Swim Framework
sources.note: Swim England's Learn to Swim Framework. Names nine core aquatic skills, taught through games rather than strokes, which is why stage 1 here has no swimming in it.
sources.$note:
The nine, as the page lists them: Entry, Exits, Floatation and Balance, Rotation and Orientation, Streamlining, Aquatic Breathing, Travel and Coordination, Water Safety, Health and Fitness.
